title: Attack Surface Management
summary: Attack surface management is the continuous process of discovering, inventorying, prioritising and reducing the set of ways an adversary can reach or influence an organisation. It has two halves that are often confused. External attack surface management discovers what is actually reachable from the internet, including forgotten subdomains, stale DNS records, exposed management interfaces, cloud storage and leaked credentials, and compares that reality with the official asset register. Internal reduction work removes unnecessary services, closes unused ports, limits standing privilege and shrinks the number of paths an intruder can use after initial access. The discipline matters because you cannot harden an asset you do not know exists, and because shadow IT, self service cloud and mergers keep the real perimeter moving away from the documented one. The mistake is commissioning a one-off scan and filing the report; the value comes from a repeating discovery loop that assigns every asset an owner and feeds remediation back into the register.

beginner.definition: Attack surface management is the work of finding and reducing the ways an attacker can reach your systems. The attack surface is everything an outsider can see or touch. It includes servers, web addresses, cloud storage and old forgotten pages. Management means keeping a live list and closing what you do not need.
beginner.whyItMatters: You cannot protect a system you do not know exists. Teams forget test servers, old subdomains and public storage. Attackers scan for exactly those forgotten things. Forgotten systems are usually less well maintained than the ones on the official list. Finding them before an attacker does is the whole point.
howItWorks: You collect every asset of your organisation that faces the public internet.
This list includes domains, subdomains, address ranges, certificates and cloud storage buckets.
Each asset is given an owner, so one person is responsible for it.
You check what each asset exposes, such as open ports or old software.
You remove what is not needed and harden the rest with patches and settings.
The search repeats on a schedule, because new assets appear all the time.
beginner.example: Think of a large hotel with hundreds of doors. The manager keeps a list of every key and who holds it. Over the years staff copy keys and forget to return them. A careful manager walks the building and finds doors that should not open at all. Attack surface management is that walk, repeated every month.
takeaways: Discover first, because unknown assets cannot be protected or patched.
Give every discovered asset a named owner and a review date.
Repeat the search regularly, since new systems appear without warning.

objectives: Explain what the attack surface is and how it grows over time.
Describe how external discovery finds assets missing from the official register.
Explain why asset ownership is required before remediation can happen.
Distinguish external exposure reduction from internal privilege and service reduction.
Describe how attack surface findings feed a vulnerability management process.
